passage:
It was sports week in December, and the Class 5 boys were sitting on the school steps in their sweaters, arguing about cricket.
"Rohit Bhandare is the best batsman in the world," Tejas said. "He hit a hundred against the toughest team. And that sixty in the final!"
Pankaj frowned. "He got out for zero three times last month."
"The umpire was blind. Everyone knows."
"And the two ducks before that?"
"Bad luck. The pitch was wet."
"So when he scores, it's him, and when he doesn't, it's the umpire?"
Tejas crossed his arms. "You don't understand cricket."
Their PT teacher, passing by with the whistle, asked what the fight was about. Tejas listed every big innings he could remember, one after another. He couldn't think of a single bad one.

qa.q: How many times did Rohit Bhandare get out for zero last month, according to Pankaj?
qa.a: Pankaj said he got out for zero three times last month.

qa.q: Why does Tejas blame the umpire and the wet pitch?
qa.a: Tejas feels loyal and proud of his hero, so good scores feel like proof and bad ones feel unfair, which keeps his belief comfortable.

qa.q: What could help Tejas see his favourite player more fairly?
qa.a: He could write down the scores of the last ten matches, good and bad, and look at them together with Pankaj.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Tejas's arguments?
qa.a: Pankaj finds them one-sided and a bit frustrating, pointing out that Tejas credits the player for runs and blames others for failures.

grounding: It shows a child who insists his favourite cricketer is the best, remembering only the big innings and blaming the umpire or luck for failures.

passage:
Diwali break, day 3
I'm Varun, and I've decided Saurabh is fake. Everyone thinks he's so nice, but I saw him laughing with the seniors right after telling me he hates them.
Since then I've been reading the class group chat with that in mind. When he wrote "great match yesterday" to Rohan, I thought: sucking up. When he posted a Diwali photo with the whole group, I thought: showing off.
He also wished me "Happy Diwali" personally this morning. I didn't open it properly. I just saw the notification and scrolled past.
The weird thing is, my video feed keeps showing me clips about "signs your friend is fake." I watched six tonight. They all fit him.
Or maybe I'm just looking for them to fit. I don't know. It's late.

qa.q: What did Saurabh send the narrator this morning?
qa.a: He wished Varun "Happy Diwali" personally.

qa.q: Why does reading the chat this way feel reasonable to Varun?
qa.a: Varun feels hurt and suspicious after seeing Saurabh laugh with the seniors, so every message seems like more proof, while friendly ones get skipped.

qa.q: What could Varun try to test the belief about Saurabh?
qa.a: Varun could open and read Saurabh's Diwali message properly, list friendly things Saurabh has done too, and maybe ask Saurabh directly about the seniors.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel if his Diwali wish goes unanswered?
qa.a: Saurabh might feel confused and a bit hurt, not knowing why Varun has gone quiet.

grounding: It shows a teenager who has decided a classmate is fake reading every message as proof, skipping the friendly ones, while the video feed serves more of the same.

passage:
Placement mentor's note, Navratri week — Noor
Kavitha, final-year commerce, has decided not to sit for campus placements. She plans to prepare for a design course abroad instead.
She came to me today with a folder she called her "research." It had eleven articles about people who skipped placements and succeeded, and notes from three seniors who did the same. When I asked if she had spoken to anyone who regretted skipping, or read anything on the other side, she said, "Why would I? I already know what I want."
She seemed confident, even relieved, as if the folder settled it.
I told her the decision may well be right for her, but that research means looking at both sides. I have given her the names of two graduates who took a placement job first and studied design later, and asked her to talk to them before the registration closes on Friday.

qa.q: How many articles were in Kavitha's research folder?
qa.a: It had eleven articles.

qa.q: Why does Kavitha feel so sure about skipping placements?
qa.a: She feels confident and relieved because her folder is full of agreeing voices, which makes her feel well researched.

qa.q: What did the mentor do, and why is it a good countermeasure?
qa.a: The mentor gave her two graduates with a different path to talk to before Friday, so she hears the other side before deciding.

qa.q: How might the two graduates see Kavitha's plan?
qa.a: They might see value in it but also share what they gained from working first, giving her a view her folder left out.

grounding: It shows, through a mentor's note, a college student collecting only articles and advice that back her decision to skip placements, and feeling well researched.

passage:
Dear Minakshi didi,
I need your advice about Kabir, my roommate.
You know he wants to drop out and start a food-delivery app for hostels. Every time someone warns him, like the professor saying the market is crowded, or his cousin saying he'd need money he doesn't have, he waves it off. "They don't get it."
But when one senior said, "Cool idea," he quoted it for three days. He has a screenshot of every thumbs-up.
I tried arguing point by point last week. It turned into a shouting match.
So last night I tried what you told me once. I said, "Kabir, I notice you remember every yes and forget every no. Can we look at both lists together?" He went quiet. Then he said, "Okay. Maybe."
Did I do it right?
Anand

qa.q: What did the senior say that Kabir quoted for three days?
qa.a: The senior said, "Cool idea."

qa.q: How did Anand feel after the point-by-point argument turned into a shouting match?
qa.a: Anand felt worried and frustrated, which is why a gentler way of raising it with Kabir seemed necessary.

qa.q: Why did naming the pattern kindly work better than arguing?
qa.a: Saying calmly that Kabir remembers every yes and forgets every no didn't attack each belief, so Kabir could listen and agree to look at both lists.

qa.q: How might Kabir feel when Anand points out the pattern?
qa.a: Kabir might feel a bit stung but also seen, which is why he goes quiet and then says "Okay. Maybe."

grounding: It shows, in a letter, a roommate noticing a friend dismiss every warning about a startup idea while quoting each encouraging comment, and naming the pattern kindly.

passage:
"Varun, you asked about the new analyst on my team? I'm Disha, and I'll be honest, I got it wrong.
Meera joined in December, right before the year-end rush. On her second day she sent a report with the wrong date on the cover. I thought, careless. She's weak.
After that, I saw it everywhere. She asked a question in the meeting: doesn't know basics. She took ten minutes longer on a task: slow. Every small slip went into my mental file.
What I didn't notice was the good stuff. She caught an error in my forecast that would have embarrassed our whole team. She stayed late during the Christmas crunch. I told myself those were flukes.
It was only in January, when my manager praised her in front of everyone, that I looked back and saw what I'd done. The first impression was driving. I was just the passenger."

qa.q: What was wrong with Meera's report on her second day?
qa.a: It had the wrong date on the cover.

qa.q: Why did Disha's view of Meera feel reasonable at the time?
qa.a: After the first slip, Disha felt sure Meera was weak, so each small mistake seemed like confirmation, and good work felt like a fluke.

qa.q: What could Disha do to judge new colleagues more fairly?
qa.a: Disha could note both good work and slips in writing for the first month before forming a view, or ask others how the colleague is doing.

qa.q: How might Meera have experienced her first weeks under Disha?
qa.a: Meera may have felt judged and uneasy, sensing her mistakes were noticed while her good work, like catching the forecast error, was not.

grounding: It shows a young professional who decided early that a new colleague was weak reading each slip as proof and ignoring her good work, as the first impression steered later evidence.

passage:
Before: On Monday, Usha, the youngest coordinator at the NGO, was certain: the after-school reading programme should move from evenings to Saturday mornings. She had the slides ready.
During: On Wednesday, before sending the proposal, she stopped and wrote a question at the top of her notebook: What would change my mind? She answered it honestly: if parents said Saturday was their only family day, or if the older children worked on weekends. Then she went to Rukmini, the field officer who disagreed with almost everything and was usually right. "Tell me the strongest case against this." Rukmini did, for twenty minutes. Usha took notes without arguing.
After: The following Monday, she called ten parents. Four said Saturdays were impossible. Usha kept the evening sessions for older children and moved only the youngest group. Rukmini read the new plan and said, "Now that's a proposal." Usha felt proud, not defeated.

qa.q: What question did Usha write at the top of her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote, "What would change my mind?"

qa.q: How did Usha feel when Rukmini approved the new plan?
qa.a: She felt proud rather than defeated, because the disagreement had made her plan stronger.

qa.q: Which of Usha's steps protected her from only seeing what she wanted to see?
qa.a: Writing what evidence would change her mind, asking a sharp critic for the strongest counter-case and calling parents before committing.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel being asked for the case against?
qa.a: Rukmini probably feels respected and taken seriously, since her disagreement is being treated as useful information instead of an insult.

grounding: It shows a worker asking what evidence would change her mind, seeking a strong critic and hearing the best case against her plan before committing.

passage:
Teacher's note, school Christmas fair — Elizabeth
Jaya, Class 3, went to the sticker stall run by the Class 7 children. The older girl told her, "Fifty rupees for this sheet." Jaya said, "Too much!" The girl said, "Okay, thirty." Jaya's face lit up. She paid at once and ran to me, delighted: "I got twenty rupees off!"
Two stalls down, the same sticker sheets were ten rupees each. Jaya saw them on her way back and went very quiet. "But she said fifty first," she said. "Thirty was a lot less."
I didn't scold her. I sat with her and we talked about how the first number we hear can make everything after it seem cheap or dear.
Next step: on Monday, in maths, the class will play a shop game where they look at all the stalls before choosing.

qa.q: What price did the older girl first say for the sticker sheet?
qa.a: She first said fifty rupees.

qa.q: Why did thirty rupees feel like a big win to Jaya?
qa.a: She felt delighted because the first price of fifty made thirty seem cheap, even though it was still more than the other stall.

qa.q: What did the teacher plan, and why is it a good countermeasure?
qa.a: A shop game where children look at all the stalls before choosing, so they compare real prices instead of judging from the first number.

qa.q: How might the older girl at the stall see the bargain?
qa.a: She probably felt pleased, since starting at fifty let her sell at thirty while Jaya felt she had won.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a child treating the first sticker price as the fair baseline, so a lower price felt like a win though it was still too high.

passage:
The monsoon rain was so heavy on results day that the school postponed the prize ceremony, and Hemant waited under the leaking bus shelter with his marks card in a plastic bag. Maths: 70.
In the first unit test he had got 90. Now 70 felt like falling off a cliff. He had been so sure. He kept seeing the 90 in his head, and the 70 looked worse each time.
His friend Kamal came splashing over, grinning. "Sixty-eight! My first test was fifty. I'm so happy!"
Hemant stared at him. Kamal's 68 was lower than his 70, and Kamal was celebrating. Hemant felt like hiding.
"You got seventy?" Kamal said. "That's great."
"It's terrible," Hemant said. "I got ninety last time."
The bus came, late and crowded. All the way home, pressed against the wet window, he kept measuring 70 against that 90.

qa.q: What did Hemant get in the first unit test?
qa.a: He had got 90 in the first unit test.

qa.q: Why does Hemant feel terrible about 70 while Kamal is happy with 68?
qa.a: Hemant feels disappointed and ashamed because his first score of 90 set the yardstick, so 70 looks like a fall, while Kamal measures from 50.

qa.q: What could help Hemant judge his result more fairly?
qa.a: He could look at what the 70 shows about the chapters he found hard, and compare it with the class average or the paper's difficulty, not just his first score.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel when Hemant calls 70 terrible?
qa.a: Kamal might feel a bit awkward or deflated, since his own 68 was a proud result for him.

grounding: It shows a teenager who scored 70 after a first test of 90 feeling terrible, while a friend is happy with less, because the first result became his yardstick.

passage:
Looking back at last Diwali, when I got my first job offer, I can see exactly where I went wrong. I'm Preeti, and the HR person opened with, "We're thinking of four lakh a year."
I had read that freshers in my field usually got between five and six. But the moment I heard four, that number sat in my head. I asked for four and a half, and when she said "four-twenty," I felt like I'd won something.
The same month, looking for a flat, the first broker said fifteen thousand. I bargained him to thirteen and felt clever. Later I found similar flats nearby for ten.
My senior Zubin laughed kindly when I told him. "They say the first number, and you bargain from their number, not from what you know."
Now, before any conversation like that, I write down the range I've found from real research, and I start from there.

qa.q: What figure did the HR person first mention?
qa.a: The HR person first said four lakh a year.

qa.q: Why did four-twenty feel like a win to Preeti?
qa.a: Preeti felt pleased because the first figure of four became the reference point, so a small rise over it felt like success even though it was below the usual range.

qa.q: What does Preeti now do before such conversations, and why does it help?
qa.a: Preeti writes down a range found through real research and starts from there, so the other side's opening number doesn't set the baseline; checking with the placement cell or a trusted senior also helps.

qa.q: How might the broker have seen the flat bargain?
qa.a: The broker probably felt satisfied, since starting at fifteen made thirteen feel generous while it was still above other flats nearby.

grounding: It shows a graduate who adjusted too little from the first salary offer and the first quoted rent, as the opening figures pulled the final agreements toward themselves.

passage:
Thursday
Today's vendor meeting taught me something. I'm Hemant, and I went along with Gargi to negotiate the printing contract.
The vendor spoke first. "For this volume, eight lakh." From then on, everything circled that number. Gargi countered with seven. They met at seven and a half. Everyone shook hands.
Back at the office, I checked the three quotes we'd got last year for the same work. They were between five and six lakh.
I told Gargi. She groaned. "He said eight so confidently, I just worked down from there." She wasn't careless. She's sharp. The first number just pulled everyone toward it, including me, and I said nothing in the room.
So next time I'm doing it differently. Before the meeting, I'll write our own range from research, bring the old quotes, and if they open high, I'll say our number and the reason, not just a smaller version of theirs.

qa.q: What range were last year's three quotes for the same work?
qa.a: They were between five and six lakh.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel after checking last year's quotes?
qa.a: Hemant felt uneasy and a little frustrated, realising the first number had pulled everyone in, including Hemant, who said nothing in the room.

qa.q: What is Hemant's plan for the next negotiation?
qa.a: Hemant will prepare a range from research, bring the old quotes and answer a high opening with their own number and reasons, not just a smaller version of the vendor's figure.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel when she heard about the old quotes?
qa.a: Gargi groaned, feeling annoyed with herself for working down from the vendor's confident eight lakh.

grounding: It shows a colleague noticing that whoever names the first figure shapes a negotiation, and planning to prepare a researched range beforehand.
